beats.prose:
The scan rolled across the console in a slow blue arc, the same arc it had drawn ten thousand times before, sweeping the void between Kael and nothing. He watched it without watching. The Iron Ghost hummed around him at the pitch he knew by the bone — that flat A below middle C the starboard coil settled into when the reactor was running cool — and the hum and the arc and the cold metal under his elbows were the morning, the way other men had coffee.

Sector seven. Empty. Sector eight. Empty.

He logged each one with a flick of his eye, the implant reading the saccade and stamping the field clean. Numbers spooled down the inside of his vision in a column so familiar he no longer read them, only felt them moving, the way a man on a long road feels the white lines without counting.

A pellet of frozen something tumbled across the edge of the screen. Ice. Not worth a course correction. He let it go.

The galley smelled of yesterday's protein and the brown rind of coffee burned onto the heater plate. He didn't get up. The chair held him the way it had been shaped to, a long groove in the cheap foam where his weight had lived for seven years. On the bulkhead above the console, the patches — Third Recon, Ganymede Free Op, a scorched corner where a name used to be — had faded to the colour of old teeth.

Sector nine. Empty.

Then the static.

It came in under the hum, not louder, only different — a hairline crack of noise across the implant's clean channel, and for the half-second it lasted he heard, or didn't hear, something on the other side of it. A pitch. A shape of a pitch. The shape a man's voice makes when it is no longer a voice.

He held very still.

The static cleared. The arc kept sweeping. His pulse, which he checked the way he checked the reactor, was steady — sixty-two, sixty-three — and he made a note in the maintenance log without looking down. *Implant: minor interference, sector nine. Recalibrate at next dock.* He had written the same line, with small variations, eleven times this year. He did not count them. The implant counted them. He had told it once to stop showing him the total.

Outside, the belt turned its slow black turn. Inside, the cabin was the temperature of a hand. He drank from the cup at his elbow without tasting it and pulled the scan forward into sector ten.

Empty.

This was the work. Stay in the chair. Stay in the arc. Keep the column moving. A man in motion was a man who could not be found by what stood still inside him, and Kael Voss had been in motion, by his own private measure, for seven years and three months and a number of days he did not let himself know.

The arc swept on. He let it. He was very good at letting it.

Sector eleven came up empty and then it didn't.

He felt it before the console said it — a hitch in the column of numbers, the smallest stutter in the rhythm he had been not-reading. His eyes went down. The implant brought the field forward on its own, anticipating him, and there it was at the bottom of sector eleven: a single returning pulse where the void should have given back nothing.

He waited for it to come again. It came again.

Not the chirp of ice catching the scan at the right angle. Not the broken cough of an old corporate buoy whose battery had gone soft. A clean tick. A pause the length of a slow breath. Another tick. Another pause, the same length, to the millisecond — he could feel the implant measuring it against itself, finding no drift.

Rhythm.

The hairs along his forearms moved before he did. He set the cup down without looking at it and brought both hands to the console and pulled the return into the centre of the screen and asked the implant, in the wordless way he asked it things, what it was.

The implant did not know.

It was the not-knowing that stopped him. The Iron Ghost's sensor suite was old and patched and stolen from four different corporate yards, but its catalogue was deep — every registered transponder, every wreck on the Alliance lists, every wildcat beacon the Belt had ever bothered to map. The pulse came back unflagged. No carrier signature. No corporate handshake. No format the implant could read, and his implant could read formats that had been retired before he was born.

He ran it again. Same result. He widened the window and let the scan listen for thirty seconds and the pulse repeated, tick and pause and tick, the pause holding to its length the way only deliberate things hold to a length.

Old, the implant offered, in the cold sideways way it offered things it had inferred rather than known. The encryption envelope, what it could see of it, sat outside any decay curve the catalogue had on file. Not corporate-old. Not Corporate-Wars-old. Older than that. Older than the catalogue went.

He sat back. The chair creaked in the place it always creaked.

*Walk away.* The thought arrived already formed, in a voice he recognised as his own and as Hale's, the way certain thoughts had carried Hale's cadence ever since the ice. *Salvage men who chase ghost beacons end up as the next ghost beacon. Log it, drop a note for someone who doesn't have to live, sleep it off.* He had walked away from three things this year already that wanted looking at, and he had slept fine after each.

He reached for the log. His hand stopped halfway.

Tick. Pause. Tick.

He had heard a lot of signals in his life. Distress beacons screamed; corporate pings clipped; pirate lures cooed and flattered. This one did none of those things. It kept its own time, indifferent to whether anyone was listening, and that indifference was the thing that held him — the sense, absurd and immediate, of a metronome that had been running in an empty room for a very long time and would go on running whether he stood up or not.

Or — and he did not let the thought finish, but it finished anyway, in the dry undertone the implant used for his worst ideas — running until the right ear walked into the room.

He looked at his hand, still hanging short of the log key. He looked at the cup. He looked at the arc, which was halfway through sector twelve now, sweeping on as if nothing had happened, because for the arc nothing had.

"All right," he said. The word landed in the cabin and the cabin took it without comment. He had not heard his own voice in eleven days.

He pulled up the nav plot. The coordinates resolved into a point sixteen hours out at the burn rate he could afford, nineteen at the burn rate that wouldn't cost him a fuel cell he'd have to explain at the next dock. He chose nineteen. He told himself he chose nineteen for the fuel. He laid the course in and watched the implant draw the line, a thin green thread across the black, ending at nothing he could name.

A salvage run, he told the part of himself that was already standing at the back of the cabin with its arms crossed. A buoy, probably. Some pre-war science package the catalogue had lost. Strip it for the rare-earth in the housing and be back in the chair before the week was out. He had rationalised worse on thinner.

He keyed the burn. The Iron Ghost shifted under him with the small reluctant lurch she always gave when asked to be somewhere new, and the hum climbed a quarter-tone, and somewhere in his chest a thing he had been keeping very still for seven years opened one eye.

The scan kept sweeping. The pulse kept ticking. He sat in the chair he had worn the shape of and watched the green thread reach for the dark, and he did not, for once, look away.

The signal resolved into shape as the Ghost closed the distance, and Kael's breath caught in a way that surprised him—a physical thing, involuntary, the kind of response he thought he had trained out of himself years ago.

It was impossible.

Not a buoy. Not a wreck. A hull, sleek and matte-black, its surface smooth in a way nothing human had ever been smooth, as if it had been grown rather than built. Eight hundred meters at least, maybe more—the distance made it hard to judge, but his implant was already parsing the geometry, running it against every database it had ever been fed, and coming back empty every time. The shape was wrong. Not streamlined for atmosphere, not reinforced for gravity. Built for something else entirely.

Along its length, faint light pulsed. Bioluminescence. Kael watched the rhythm—a slow, patient pulse that reminded him of something breathing in its sleep. The runes beneath it were intricate, geometric, nothing like the clean angles of corporate design or the brutal functionality of military hulls. These were old. Older than the catalogue. Older than anything he had words for.

He cut the engines and let the Ghost drift, the momentum carrying them closer at a crawl. The alien structure grew in the viewport with no sign of weapons, no hail frequency, no response to the dozen frequencies he cycled through on pure instinct. Just the pulse. Just the silence.

His hands were steady on the controls. His pulse was steady. But something in his chest had shifted, a thing that lived deeper than steadiness, and he could feel it moving.

He ran a full sensor sweep. The implant wanted to reject the data—the hull composition didn't match anything, the energy signature was unlike anything it had been trained to recognize, the age estimate kept oscillating between "impossible" and "catastrophically impossible." He made himself sit with the numbers. Made himself look at them.

Forty thousand years. Approximately. The implant hedged, but that was what the decay curves were screaming when he forced them to make a decision.

He should have turned the Ghost around. Should have logged it, contacted the CDA, let someone with authority decide what to do with a ghost signal from something that had no right to exist. Should have. The word was heavy in his head, heavy and familiar and useless.

Instead, he was already moving.

The suit was in the locker where it always was, the same suit he'd worn for seven years, patched and re-patched until there was almost nothing original left about it except the name stitched into the collar—a name he didn't use anymore, from a life he didn't claim. He sealed the seals and checked the seals and checked them again, and the ritual of it steadied him the way it always did. Seal by seal, he was building a barrier between himself and whatever was happening, a structure he could survive inside.

The airlock cycled. The void opened up, absolute and black, and Kael pushed off into it.

Space had never frightened him. Space was honest—it killed you or it didn't, and there was no ambiguity in that. He kicked toward the alien hull, his suit's thrusters speaking in small bursts, and the distance collapsed with agonizing slowness. The pulse grew brighter as he approached. The runes resolved into something almost readable, patterns within patterns, a language written in light and geometry.

He reached out. His gloved hand was small against the hull, insignificant, but as his fingers made contact the warmth took him completely by surprise.

Warm. The hull was warm. In the absolute zero of the void, something that had been drifting for forty thousand years was radiating heat. His implant screamed contradiction. He pressed his palm flat against it and felt the pulse beneath the surface, steady and slow and alive.

The signal came then—not a sound but a presence, a clarity that bloomed directly into his neural implant like a door opening onto a room he didn't remember entering. Recognition. The hull recognized him. Not his body, not his suit, but something in him, something wired deep, and it knew what he was.

Kael pulled his hand back as if burned, but the connection held for a moment longer, a thread of information too vast and too strange to parse, and then it released. The pulse on the hull continued its patient rhythm, unchanged, as if it had been waiting for exactly this moment and found him exactly as expected.

He hung in the void, suspended between the Iron Ghost and the thing that had just touched him back. Behind his sternum, something was waking up. Something that had been asleep for seven years and three months in a chair worn smooth by his own weight.

The airlock to the alien vessel was twenty meters away. He could see it now—a geometric impossibility, a door that wasn't quite a door, a shape that hurt to look at directly. His implant was still cycling through responses, still finding nothing to compare this against. Still certain, in its cold precision, that none of this should be possible.

Kael fired his thrusters and moved toward the opening. The point of no return had already passed somewhere in the last few minutes, though he couldn't pinpoint exactly when. Somewhere between seeing the shape resolve in the darkness and feeling the hull recognize him. He was committed now, and the thing inside him that had just woken up didn't want to go back to sleep.

The airlock drew closer. The pulse grew brighter. And in the back of his skull, where the implant lived, something ancient began to speak in a language that predated words.

The airlock sealed behind him with a sound like a breath being drawn inward.

Inside, there was no transition. No corridor, no antechamber, no staging ground between the void and whatever waited beyond. The alien architecture did not believe in thresholds. The moment the outer door cycled shut, the inner door was already opening—or had always been open, the distinction lost somewhere in his perception—and the chamber beyond swallowed the light from his suit lamps without reflection.

Not darkness. Something else. A space so vast that the concept of walls seemed quaint, seemed almost insulting. The chamber stretched away in directions his eyes could not quite parse, up and down becoming meaningless abstractions. Floating throughout the impossible volume were structures—crystalline lattices suspended in zero-g, geometric forms that shifted at the edge of vision, becoming solid only when he looked directly at them, then dissolving back into something abstract the moment his attention moved. The air—if it could be called air—tasted of metal and ozone and something else, something his brain could not quite name but his implant was already trying to catalogue and failing.

His suit lights touched nothing and changed nothing. The structures did not reflect or absorb the beams. They existed in some register that standard illumination could not reach.

Kael cut the suit lamps and waited for his eyes to adjust. They didn't. The chamber remained as it was—not dark, but not lit, existing in a state that made the distinction between the two seem provincial. After a moment, he realized he wasn't waiting anymore. He was moving.

His thrusters were off. His suit jets weren't firing. But he was crossing the chamber nonetheless, drawn in a direction that felt less like choice and more like compliance with a current he had stepped into without seeing. His implant was screaming—a sound that had no actual sound, a sensation of cascading contradictions, everything it knew about physics and navigation colliding with the simple fact of his movement through space that should not be possible.

The device at the chamber's heart was waiting.

Kael saw it and stopped seeing anything else. A crystal, perhaps—the word seemed too small, too human, but it was the closest his vocabulary could reach. It hung at the chamber's center, a geometric perfection that made the lattices surrounding it look like crude approximations. The shape was not quite a cube, not quite a sphere, not quite anything that had three spatial dimensions. It pulsed with light—blue, deep blue, the blue of something very far and very cold—and the rhythm of that pulse matched exactly the rhythm of his heartbeat. His implant was not feeding him that information. He knew it the way he knew he was breathing. The device was matching him. Learning him. Waiting to see if he would match it back.

He reached out without deciding to reach out.

The distance between them collapsed in a way that suggested the distance had never been real—a trick of perspective, a courtesy extended and now withdrawn. His fingers—bare, he had removed the suit glove at some point, though he could not remember doing so, could not even remember seeing bare skin in the void—touched the surface of the crystal and the universe inverted.

Light was not an adequate word.

The blue became everything. It was not light that filled the chamber—it was light that became the chamber, became the air, became the space between his thoughts. His implant, which had been screaming contradictions, suddenly went silent in a way that was worse than any sound. In that silence, he felt it arrive: a presence in the neural pathways, something vast and patient and utterly indifferent to whether he lived or understood what was happening. The device was not entering his implant. It was recognizing the implant as an extension of itself, a fragment of something it had been waiting to find.

Information flooded through him. Not words. Not images. Pure data in a form his consciousness could only translate into sensation: coordinates, a map of the solar system rendered as something three-dimensional and shifting, each point marked with a number. A countdown. A timer that was not counting down to anything he could name, but counting down nonetheless, and the number was urgent, and the number was wrong.

And underneath it all, a warning. Not in language. In the bone-deep certainty that something was already moving in the dark between the stars, that it had been moving for longer than human history, and that it had just noticed the light he was shining by touching this device.

The device bonded. That was the only word for it. He felt the fusion happening at the neural level, a merging of architecture that should have been impossible, should have destroyed him outright. But his implant—his old, patched, barely-functional implant—was not rejecting it. It was welcoming it. Some part of him that he had never known existed was singing in recognition of something it had been designed to find.

The light faded. Or he faded from the light. The distinction became meaningless as the chamber returned, as his breathing returned, as the small practical sensations of his body reasserted themselves—the pressure suit against his skin, the recycled air in his lungs, the cold seeping through the suit's insulation. He was on his knees in the chamber's center, though he did not remember falling to his knees. The crystal hung before him, pulsing, patient, finished with him now that it had delivered what it came to deliver.

His hands were shaking.

Kael forced them still, forced himself to breathe in the measured way the suit's systems required, forced himself to look at what he had just become. The implant in his skull was different now—not in any way that the suit's diagnostics could measure, but in every way that mattered. Something had been woven into it. Something that knew things. Something that was waiting for him to understand what those things meant.

The countdown was still there, a phantom sensation just beneath consciousness. Hours. The timer was reading something in hours, and with each second that passed, the number decreased by one second, and somewhere in the solar system, something ancient was waking up.

Kael looked down at his trembling hands and saw them clearly for the first time since he had entered the chamber. They were his hands. Still human. Still his. But something fundamental had shifted in the moment of contact, and he knew with absolute certainty that he would never be able to go back to the salvage operator he had been. The lie of isolation had just been shattered by something older and infinitely more patient than his seven years in the void.

The device pulsed. Once. A gentle rhythm, almost like forgiveness, almost like welcome. It had found what it was looking for. And it had just put a countdown in his skull that the entire solar system was going to hear before the day was done.

The knowledge did not come as words. It came as certainty—a flood of understanding that bypassed language entirely and spoke directly to the part of his brain that still remembered how to be afraid.

He saw the solar system rendered in three dimensions that hurt to perceive, each colony marked with a symbol that pulsed like a dying heartbeat. Mars. The Belt. Europa. Titan. Each one was a node in a network, and he could see them all at once, could feel them the way a nervous system feels a hand touching fire. The coordinates were written into him now—not memorized but known, the way he knew his own name, the way a compass knows north.

And underneath the coordinates: the warning.

It was not a voice. It was a resonance that moved through his spine, a vibration in the marrow, the bone-deep certainty of something vast and patient and already in motion. Something that had been sleeping in the dark between the stars for longer than the solar system had existed. Something that had just noticed the light.

The device was not a weapon. The clarity of that struck him like a physical blow. It was a failsafe. Left behind by something that understood the cost of its own extinction, that had known—thousands of years before humanity took its first breath—that something else was coming. Something hungry. Something that did not die. The device was a beacon and a warning and a trap all at once, left in the hope that someone, someday, would wake it and be strong enough to understand what came next.

Kael was not strong enough. The knowledge arrived with that certainty too.

The countdown was still there, still running. Hours. He could feel the number decreasing with each breath, could feel the way each second that passed was one second closer to something that had already begun. And somewhere in the solar system—he could sense it now, the way an animal senses a predator—something was moving toward the inner planets, drawn by the pulse of the device the way a shark is drawn by blood in the water.

The visions fractured. The chamber dissolved back into geometry and empty space. Kael found himself gasping, on his knees, his suit's respirator working overtime to keep pace with the panic his body was refusing to acknowledge. His hands were pressed against the cold floor of the chamber—or they had never left it, or they had always been there. Time was becoming unreliable in ways his implant couldn't quantify.

He forced himself to look up. The crystal was still there, still pulsing, still waiting. It had delivered its message. It was done with him now.

But he was not done with it. And more importantly: it was not done with the solar system.

Kael's vision blurred. Not tears—he was not capable of tears anymore, hadn't been for seven years—but something close. His implant was burning, a sensation of heat that had no source and no mercy. He could feel the new architecture settling into place, feel the way the device had rewired something fundamental in the way he perceived reality. He was not the same person who had touched the crystal. That person had been alone, had been safe in his isolation, had been able to pretend that his distance from the human race was a choice rather than a prison.

That person was gone.

What remained was something else: a messenger carrying a countdown that the entire solar system would hear before the day was done. The corporations would know. The colonies would know. And somewhere in the vast dark, something ancient and patient and utterly indifferent to human survival would know that its failsafe had been triggered, that the warning had been sent, that the final act was beginning whether anyone was ready or not.

Kael pulled himself to his feet, his suit's servos hissing with the effort. The chamber was already fading now, the crystalline lattices becoming translucent, the vast impossible space collapsing back into something almost comprehensible. The device had no more use for him. It had made him what it needed him to be.

He walked toward the airlock—or was carried there, the distinction no longer clear. His legs moved because they had to move. His hands moved to seal the suit because the suit demanded to be sealed. The small rituals of survival that had sustained him through seven years of solitude were still there, still functioning, but they felt like the movements of a ghost now, the memory of a man who no longer existed.

The airlock cycled. The void opened up again, honest and black and utterly indifferent.

Kael pushed off toward the Iron Ghost, and as he drifted through the darkness, he could feel the countdown continuing its inexorable descent. Hours now. Maybe less. The device was already broadcasting—he could sense it, a pulse radiating out through the solar system at the speed of light, carrying a message that every neural implant would translate into pure, undeniable terror.

He had come to this place looking for salvage.

He was leaving as something that could never be salvaged.

The Iron Ghost's comms system was picking up fragments—a woman's voice, clipped and professional, saying something about pressure cascading through the lower domes, then nothing. Static. Then a man's voice underneath, lower, almost inaudible: "They're not responding. The neural feeds are—" and then that too cut into white noise that sounded like screaming translated into mathematics.

Kael sat in the command chair with his hands flat on the armrests, watching the data scroll across his displays. The ship's systems had no context for what they were seeing. To the Iron Ghost's instruments, Europa Station was simply going dark—life support failing, comms arrays frying in sequence, neural network collapsing like a building with its supports cut out. Standard catastrophe. The kind of thing that happened in the outer system when you trusted your survival to corporate infrastructure and corporate infrastructure decided to fail.

He knew better.

The coordinates the device had shown him included Europa. Not as a target. As a node. A point in the network. And the countdown—he could still feel it, a phantom timer just beneath his consciousness—had been running for eight hours and forty-three minutes when he had touched the crystal. Now it was eight hours and thirty-two minutes. And the failsafe was spreading.

The news feeds picked it up first. Nexus Prime's official statement, released in the time it took Kael to watch the signal cascade across the system: catastrophic systems failure at Europa Research Station. Cause under investigation. All neural implants in the colony experiencing unprecedented cascade failure. Communication protocols being established with survivors.

There would be no survivors.

Kael watched the feeds update in real time. The investigation was already being spun. Corporate Defense Alliance was already mobilizing. And somewhere in the cascade of data, he could feel it—the moment they realized what had actually happened. Not a systems failure. Not a cascade. An overwrite. Someone had taken control of every neural implant in the colony simultaneously and erased the human beings running them. Seven hundred and forty-three people. Gone. Not dead. Erased. The distinction was important. Death left a body. This left nothing but empty meat and a lot of questions that nobody in the corporate structure wanted to ask.

His implant was burning again. The new architecture settling into place was pulling data from the Europa feeds, translating them into something his consciousness could process. He could feel the moment the signal had hit the colony. Could feel the shape of it, the way it had moved through the neural network like a predator moving through water. Clean. Efficient. Absolute.

And he had woken it.

The realization moved through him slowly, the way cold moves through a body. Not sudden. Inevitable. Like watching a chain reaction that was always going to happen, finally happening. Seven years of running. Seven years of isolation, of refusing crew, of telling himself that distance kept people safe. And in seven years, he had managed to preserve exactly nothing. The colonies had gone on about their business. The corporations had gone on extracting resources and consolidating power. The outer rim independents had gone on scraping survival from the void. And he had gone on salvaging, drifting, believing that his solitude meant he wasn't responsible for any of it.

The device had been waiting in the Kuiper Belt for forty thousand years. It had not cared about his isolation. It had cared about the one thing in the solar system with a neural implant old enough, damaged enough, and desperate enough to recognize it. It had found him not because he was safe but because he was the only one broken enough to be useful.

Seven hundred and forty-three people. The number was scrolling across his displays now, the corporate feeds updating with survivor counts that kept dropping, kept approaching zero. Family names. Service records. Genetic profiles for the corporate databases. All of it useless now. All of it ash in the solar wind.

Kael cut the feeds. The silence that followed felt like another kind of screaming.

His hands were still shaking. They had been shaking since he had left the alien chamber, and no amount of force of will had managed to still them. The tremor was coming from deeper than muscle now. It was coming from the part of him that understood the shape of what he had done. Not intentionally. Not with any malice. But done nonetheless. He had answered a beacon. He had touched a device. And in the moment of contact, he had set a countdown running that had just claimed seven hundred and forty-three lives in the time it took for light to travel from the Jupiter system to the inner planets.

The Iron Ghost's systems were already flagging him. Nexus Prime's security network had him on passive scan. They would know soon, if they didn't already know. A salvage operator drifting in the deep Kuiper Belt. A man with no crew, no corporate affiliation, no legitimate reason to be anywhere near an ancient derelict. The pattern would assemble itself in the corporate intelligence systems. By morning, he would be a suspect. By nightfall, he would be a terrorist.

Which was fine. Which was what he deserved.

But it was not fine for anyone else. That was the part that cut deepest. The part that took the lie of seven years of isolation and showed it for what it was: not protection but procrastination. He had told himself that staying alone kept people safe. That refusing to lead or trust anyone meant nobody would die because of him. And he had been wrong. Dead wrong. The kind of wrong that seven hundred and forty-three people couldn't come back from.

The countdown was still running. Eight hours and nineteen minutes. And somewhere in the solar system, something ancient and patient was moving closer, drawn by the pulse of the device the way all predators are drawn by the scent of blood in the water.

Kael pulled up the trajectory data. Three more colonies were in the signal's path. Mars. The Belt stations. Titan. All of them would be in range within the hour if the failsafe continued to spread at its current velocity. All of them would go dark the same way Europa had gone dark. All of them would have their own survivor counts, their own family names scrolling across the news feeds, their own moment of absolute erasure.

Unless.

The thought arrived before he could stop it. Unless he did something. Unless he got off this ship, got to one of those colonies, got to someone who could understand what was happening and how to stop it. Unless he broke the most fundamental rule he had set for himself—the rule that said staying alone was the only way to keep anyone safe.

Seven years of isolation had bought him nothing but a countdown in his skull and the blood of seven hundred and forty-three people on his hands.

It was time to try something else.
